title: Coherent migration of the single excitation injected into finite-length segment of the biomolecular chain
authors: D. Chevizovich, V. Matic, Z. Przulj, S. Galovic
abstract: We study the migration of a single excitation excited at a structural element of a finite molecular segment, which is a part of a long biomolecular chain. The excitation cannot leave the segment and is locally coupled to thermal vibrations of the lattice, forming a self-trapped state corresponding to a nonadiabatic polaron. The time-dependent probability distribution of finding the excitation at the nodes of the segment is calculated, with particular emphasis on the role of the initial excitation position. A formal analogy is observed between the present model and continuous-time quantum walk models on finite chains with reflecting boundaries. The results reveal an asymmetry in the probability distribution for nodes symmetrically positioned with respect to the initially excited site, which arises solely from the asymmetric placement of the initial excitation within the finite segment. The only exception occurs when the initially excited node is located at the center of the segment, where the probability distribution becomes symmetric. The complex interference pattern and the absence of well-defined revivals stem from the non-equidistant spectrum of mode frequencies, leading to progressive dephasing of the constituent modes. As a result, the initially well-localized probability maximum fragments into one dominant maximum accompanied by several secondary maxima of lower intensity. These findings highlight the importance of boundary conditions and initial-state geometry in controlling quantum transport in finite molecular systems.
summary: This paper theoretically analyzes how a single excitation moves coherently within a finite segment of a biomolecular chain. It shows that the migration dynamics are dominated by complex quantum interference patterns rather than simple classical diffusion. Crucially, it reveals that boundary conditions and the initial placement of the excitation induce measurable asymmetries in the probability distribution.
main_problem: The study investigates the coherent migration of a single excitation injected into a finite segment of a biomolecular chain.
main_result: The probability distribution exhibits an asymmetry for symmetrically placed nodes, which is solely due to the initial asymmetric placement within the finite boundary. The dynamics are governed by quantum interference rather than classical propagation.
method: The analysis involves solving time-dependent equations of motion derived from a modified Holstein model using techniques like Laplace transforms and relating the problem to continuous-time quantum walk models.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as a finite molecular segment (MS) within a biomolecular chain, described by an adapted Holstein Hamiltonian coupling electronic excitations to lattice vibrations. The excitation forms a self-trapped state resembling a nonadiabatic polaron.
key_observables: Time-dependent probability distribution of the excitation at nodes ($p_n(t)$), asymmetry in this distribution, and interference patterns.
important_parameters: The initial excitation position ($n_0$), boundary conditions (finite length $K$), and dimensionless parameters related to coupling strength ($S$) and hopping ($B$).
main_assumptions: The model assumes the excitation cannot leave the finite segment, employs a Lang-Firsov unitary transformation, and uses a mean-field approximation that neglects incoherent polaron–phonon scattering.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the Time-Probability Spectrum (TPS) showing deviations from symmetry at later times due to boundary effects, and demonstrate how the probability distribution evolves based on whether the initial excitation site is central or off-center.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model using a modified Holstein Hamiltonian; it then applies polaron transformations and mean-field approximations to derive equations of motion for the correlation functions. The core analysis focuses on solving these equations to determine the time evolution, highlighting geometric effects like boundary asymmetry.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed quantum mechanical description of energy transport in nanoscale biological systems, bridging concepts from polaron physics and quantum walks to explain non-trivial spatial localization effects governed by geometry.

FIG. 3. A schematic illustration of the rule allowing one to obtain V (L) n (x) for a (M, N) structure, from V (R) n (x) of the corresponding (M ′ = N, N ′ = M) structure.

FIG. 4. TPS corresponding to the two nearest-neighbor sites of the initially excited site in a MS with M = 4, N = 16 (K = 21) SEs.
